activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, so a drop of vinegar makes it fizz as carbon dioxide gas is released.
story:
The planetarium classroom smelled like dust and old carpet, and Hailey stared at the three unlabeled rocks on her tray while Ms. Becker wrote igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic on the board. On Monday each student had to sort five mystery rocks and defend every choice, and Hailey still could not tell them apart. Camila next to her kept turning a gray lump over and over like it might whisper its origin.

"That one's got bubbles in it," Jeremi said from across the table. "Bubbles means volcanic, right? Igneous." He said it with total confidence, and Hailey almost copied him, because Jeremi's dad worked in plumbing and Jeremi claimed to know how everything hidden worked, pipes, wires, rocks. But when she held the lump near the lamp, the bubbles looked stretched and flat, not round, as if the rock had melted and folded rather than bubbled. "I think it changed after it formed," she said slowly. "Like something squashed and heated it until it transformed into something new." Jeremi shrugged. "Metamorphic, then. Whatever."

The third rock was pale and layered, and nobody could decide. Hailey was about to guess sedimentary when she remembered her lunch bag. The vinegar bottle for her sandwich crinkle-crinkled in her hand as she carried the rock to the sink, and she let one drop fall onto its surface. For a second nothing happened. Ms. Becker paused at the board. Camila leaned in, breath held.

Then the wet spot hissed and fizzed, tiny bubbles crowding up like a shaken soda. "Whoa," Jeremi said. "It's alive?"

"It's limestone," Hailey said. "Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, and vinegar makes it fizz because it releases carbon dioxide gas." She had read it in the quarry chapter two weeks ago and almost forgotten. "If it fizzes, it's limestone, so it's sedimentary. It settled in layers, that's why the stripes." She wrote sedimentary beside the rock and underlined it twice.

Ms. Becker looked over her shoulder at the fizzing drop and said nothing, but one corner of her mouth lifted. On the tray, the last unknown rock sat quiet and dark, waiting.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Fractures of the radius near the wrist are the most common fractures seen in children, and they usually happen from falling onto an outstretched hand.
story:
Kaitlyn sat on the low wall by the basketball courts, her right arm propped on her knee inside its hard blue cast. The cast ran from below her elbow to her knuckles, and it had been there for three weeks, ever since she had gone over the handlebars of her bike and thrown her hands out in front of her. Dr. Ortiz had said the break was in her radius, the big bone on the thumb side, near the wrist, and that breaks like hers were the most common kind kids got, usually from landing on an outstretched hand.

Across the playground, Alden was rolling toward the ramp on his new skateboard, and Kaelyn was jogging beside him with the stopwatch from the gym bin. "The talent show tryouts are right after lunch," Kaelyn called over. "You've got one recess left to land it."

Kaitlyn chewed the inside of her cheek. Alden had fallen twice already this morning, and both times he had stuck his arms out straight, palms forward, exactly the way she had done off her bike. She could not see what would happen if he fell again. Nobody could. But she had started noticing a pattern in the way kids fell on this playground, and she wanted to test it before the bell rang.

She raised her good arm and waved them over. "Alden, do me a favor. Fall down on the grass. On purpose, so you're ready for it."

He rolled his eyes, but the bell deadline was close, so he hopped off the board and let himself tip sideways onto the soft grass beside the courts. He tucked his arm and rolled onto his shoulder. Then she asked him to fall the other way, arms out like most people do when they are surprised. This time his hand slapped down first, and all his weight drove straight through the wrist. He sat up and shook out his fingers. "That one felt way worse," he admitted.

"That's what I did," Kaitlyn said. She tapped the cast with her left hand. "Radius, right near the wrist. The doctor said that's the most common break in kids, and it usually happens exactly like what you just did." She kept her voice level, not panicked, because Alden looked a little pale now. "So the problem isn't falling. It's what your hands do when you don't have time to think."

Ms. Sharma, on yard duty near the fence, wandered over with her coffee. "Everything cooperating out here?" she asked, and Kaitlyn said yes, just an experiment. The motivation was simple: Alden's tryout was in twenty minutes, and a trip to the emergency room would end it before it started. Kaitlyn laid out her plan. Alden would practice the tucked roll until his body did it without thinking, so that if the board shot out from under him, a bad wrist would not be the probable outcome.

They used the last ten minutes of recess on the grass, again and again, until Alden could drop and roll smoothly with his arms pulled in. When the bell rang, he stood up with grass in his hair and climbed onto the board.

At the tryout, the board wobbled on the ramp's lip, and Alden pitched forward. He tucked, rolled, and came up standing in the wood chips with his hands empty and whole.

"See you at the show," Kaelyn said, and Alden grinned and held up both open palms to Kaitlyn, all ten fingers wiggling.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
story:
Arthur sat cross-legged on the living room rug with his tablet balanced on a stack of board games, scowling at two headlines side by side. Ms. Mwangi's class project was due Monday, and the assignment was to compare how two news stories covered the same event: a downtown crowd that had blocked traffic for three hours on Saturday. One headline said "Protesters March for Clean Water." The other said "Rioters Snarl City Streets." He and Elie had agreed to split the work, but Elie's part sat untouched in his messages, and Arthur could not figure out what the two stories even had in common.

Aleah arrived after dinner, still holding her basketball shoes by the laces, because Elie had texted her that Arthur was stuck. She flopped onto the couch and pulled the tablet onto her knees. "Same day, same street, same number of people?" she said. "Then it's the same crowd." She tapped the first headline. "So why do I want to be on their side when I read this one, and kind of scared when I read that one?"

Arthur read both articles out loud, and something strange happened. Reading the word "protesters," he pictured his neighbor holding a sign about the river. Reading "rioters," he pictured shattered glass, even though the second article never mentioned any glass breaking at all. He sat back. "It's the words," he said slowly. "The words are doing something."

He grabbed a napkin from the coffee table and wrote two columns. Above the first he put "Protesters" and above the second "Rioters," then he copied every word that described the crowd from each article. The first story used "passionate," "united," and "neighbors." The second used "mob," "aggressive," and "lawless." None of the words were lies exactly, but each one carried a feeling that pushed him somewhere. He tried swapping them, putting "passionate" into the second article, and the crowd suddenly sounded brave instead of dangerous. Same facts, opposite feeling. He could almost deduce the rule from it, like solving for a missing number, but he wanted to be sure before he claimed it. It was probable that the words carried strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" could push readers toward opposite opinions, but probable was not certain.

"Test it," Aleah said. "Do it like Ms. Mwangi's simile thing from poetry, where the same idea feels different depending on the picture." So they wrote one plain sentence on the napkin: "A crowd gathered on Fifth Street." Then they read it to Arthur's dad in the kitchen twice, first with "the brave protesters" added and then with "the dangerous rioters." After the first version, his dad said he hoped the city listened to them. After the second, he asked whether anyone got hurt. Same sentence, same man, opposite reaction.

Aleah laughed so hard she dropped a shoe. Arthur copied both versions of the sentence into his project notes and wrote one line underneath: "Check the word before you trust the feeling." Then he texted Elie: bring snacks Monday, and bring your part, because we actually found something. From the kitchen his dad called, "Who's brave and dangerous out there?" and Arthur held up the napkin. "Everyone," he said. "Depends what you call them."

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: A waxing crescent is lit on the right side as seen from the Northern Hemisphere, but on the left side as seen from the Southern Hemisphere.
story:
Florence pushed the desk lamp into the middle of her grandfather's den and set a striped beach ball on top of a stool. "Grandpa, can you be the Earth?" she asked. "I have to show the Moon phases for Mr. Somsak's class, and I need somebody standing in the middle." Her grandfather settled onto a kitchen chair beside the stool, holding his teacup like a prop. He had been telling her all morning about how he'd paid off the mortgage on this very house before her mother was even born, and now he was glad for a new subject. "One small step for Grandpa," he said, planting his slippers firmly on the rug.

Florence dimmed the curtains and clicked the lamp on. The room went dark except for that one bright point. She walked the beach ball in a slow circle around her grandfather, watching the stripey sphere catch the light. Half of it was always lit, she noticed, but from where Grandpa sat, the lit part changed shape. When the ball swung to his right side, he raised a finger. "I see a crescent," he announced, "and it's bright on the right."

"That's a waxing crescent," Florence said. She marked the spot on the rug with a sticky note so she could find it again, then kept circling, calling out each shape as Grandpa reported it. That was when her grandfather's tablet buzzed. It was the weekly call to her cousin in Australia, and he propped it on the shelf so everyone could see. On screen, her cousin waved from a balcony, and behind her, hanging in a deep blue evening sky, was the actual Moon.

Florence leaned close to the screen. "Is that a crescent?" she asked. Her cousin turned to look. "Yes, just getting bigger," she said. "It's waxing." Florence frowned at the little luminous sliver on the screen, then back at her beach ball. On the tablet the lit side was on the left. Around Grandpa's chair, it had been on the right. She grabbed the tablet, held it up beside her model, and looked from one to the other until her neck ached.

"Wait," she said slowly. "We're in the Northern Hemisphere. My cousin's in the Southern Hemisphere. A waxing crescent is lit on the right side as seen from the Northern Hemisphere, but on the left side as seen from the Southern Hemisphere." Her cousin, hearing all this from ten thousand kilometres away, held her tablet up to the real Moon again so Florence could double-check. Left side. Definitely left. Florence spun the beach ball and stood on her toes to peer up from underneath it, tilting her head like someone standing upside down on the far side of the world.

"Grandpa, lean sideways," she said, pulling his elbow. "Pretend you're in Australia." He tipped sideways in his chair, nearly spilling his tea, and squinted at the beach ball. "Well, I'll be," he said. "It's backwards from here." Florence wrote it all down in her notebook for Mr. Somsak, then held the tablet up next to her model one more time and grinned at her cousin. "Tomorrow, show Calder," her cousin said. "Make him lean."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real feeding relationships form a food web of many linked chains rather than one single chain.
story:
Paisley crouched at the edge of the community garden pond with her clipboard, drawing arrows in pencil. The garden tour started at noon and Mr. Cruz wanted every poster finished by eleven, so she had two hours to make her food chain look perfect: sun, then pond plants, then snails, then a duck. Simple. She had copied it off the board in science class, and Mr. Cruz had said a chain had to run from the sun all the way to a top predator. "Done," she said, and held it up for Laura, who was labeling the tomato beds nearby.

Laura leaned over, then squinted at the water. "Wait. Watch the duck." The duck was paddling along the shallow edge, and Paisley watched it tip forward, tail in the air. It nibbled at the green strands hanging from the rocks, and then it snapped at something small and brown. Henri, who was weeding the lettuce, came over and pointed. "That's a snail. It just ate one of your snails. And before that it ate the plants." Paisley stared at her neat chain of arrows. If the duck ate the plants too, then her drawing was wrong. One of her arrows was missing, and if one arrow could be missing, maybe more were.

"So what do I do, put a second arrow from the plants to the duck?" she asked. "Then it's not a chain anymore. It's got a loop in it." She tried sketching it, and the arrows crossed each other and made the whole poster look sinister, like a spider had crawled across her page. Henri tapped the water where a small fish darted past. "That fish probably eats snails too. And maybe the plants." Paisley added the fish and drew its arrows, then wondered whether the duck ate the fish, and whether something ate the duck. Her page filled with lines going every direction. "It's not a chain," she said slowly. "It's a web. Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so it's all linked."

At ten fifty she drew the final version in marker, arrows crossing like string between her fingers. Then she tested the idea Mr. Cruz had asked about, what happens if one link disappears. She imagined the snails gone. The duck would still live, because it had the plants and the fish. But the fish would go hungry, and if the fish starved, whatever ate the fish would starve too. She wrote that in her corner box and walked her poster to the shed, conserving her last blank page in case Mr. Cruz wanted a redo. He read it twice and grinned. "A web," he said. "Better than a chain." Paisley pointed at the duck, still tipping upside down in the shallows, still eating everything it could reach.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A traditional corded phone on a copper landline usually keeps working in a power cut, because the phone company powers the line, but cordless phones need household electricity.
story:
The lights went out at the farmhouse just as Jack sat down to dinner, and the wind outside made the whole blackout feel like it had been planned rather than random. His dad found a flashlight while Jack tried the cordless phone to call Ema, who was coming over at seven to work on their science project. The phone was dead. Not a beep, not a flicker on its little screen.

"It has to charge," his dad said from the hallway. Jack was about to resign himself to an evening without talking to anyone when he remembered the old phone bolted to the kitchen wall, the one with the curly cord his grandmother used before she moved out. Everyone joked it was there because Grandma refused to give it up, like some stubborn stereotype of a farmer who hated new gadgets. Jack lifted the heavy receiver, and there it was: a dial tone, steady and clear, even though every light in the house was dark.

"That's weird," he said aloud. The cordless one sat in its cradle, useless without electricity, but this old thing worked fine. He thought about it while punching in Ema's number. If the cordless needed the house's power, then the wall phone must be getting its power from somewhere else. He didn't know how, exactly, but the dial tone was proof enough.

Ema answered on the second ring. "Jack? Where are you calling from? Your cell keeps going to voicemail."

"The farmhouse. Power's out, and the cordless phone is dead, but the old wall phone in the kitchen still has a dial tone. The phone company must power the line itself." He heard her groan. "What's wrong?"

"My mom was going to leave right now to drop off the poster board. If she doesn't leave before the creek road floods, I can't bring anything tonight, and we present tomorrow." Ema's project, her poster, her whole grade, riding on one phone call.

"Then call her. We've got a working phone and thirty seconds. Go!"

He heard Ema take a breath, and then the quick tapping of her dialing his grandmother's old phone number from memory.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
story:
Elena sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop open, replaying the video Aliya had sent her from Tuesday's choir practice. Pierre-Olivier had been sailing along on the high note when his voice split in half, one sound for a moment and then a completely different one. Everybody had laughed, even Pierre-Olivier, but not meanly, and then Ms. Warsame had held up her hand and said something Elena had only half heard because Aliya was whispering to her at the time.

She played the clip again with her ear pressed close. There. Ms. Warsame's voice, faint under the giggling: "The larynx grows during puberty, and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, so the voice may crack while that happens." Elena paused the video and touched her own throat, feeling the small hard ridge there when she hummed. She thought about Pierre-Olivier at the spring concert, before any of this, his voice as light and steady as a flute. Now it was like a door swinging between two rooms.

She needed to know if growing longer and thicker would really do that to a sound. She dug through her desk drawer and found two rubber bands, a skinny one and a thick one, and stretched each one over the top of an empty tissue box. The box was porous cardboard, full of tiny holes, and it buzzed like a little speaker when she plucked the bands. The skinny band gave a high note. The thick band, stretched the same distance, gave a low one. Then she tried stretching the thick band slowly while plucking it, and the note slid downward and caught somewhere in the middle with a wobbly, broken sound. She played the clip one more time and plucked at the same moment, and the two cracked sounds matched almost exactly.

Aliya arrived in the doorway with her backpack still on one shoulder. "Are you seriously doing science on Pierre-Olivier's voice?"

"I'm doing science on my voice too," Elena said. "Mine is going to change eventually, just differently." She felt a small pang of resentment that the boys got a whole dramatic transformation and she got braces first, but she plucked the thick band again anyway, and the buzz came out low and croaky, like a frog learning to sing.

Aliya dropped her backpack and sat down. "Do the slidey one again," she said.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
Jordan had been to weddings before, but never one where the bride's family came from Malaysia, so he watched everything closely at the reception, because the gift he'd brought was wrapped wrong and he didn't know how wrong until he saw it. His mom had told him to hand the package to the bride's aunt at the welcome table. He'd grabbed it with his left hand, easy and natural, and the aunt had smiled but not taken it. She had waited, palm open, until Jordan noticed that every single guest ahead of him had used their right hand to give envelopes and boxes.

He switched hands. She received the gift with her right hand and pressed her own right palm briefly to her chest, and Jordan stepped aside feeling like he'd almost dropped something important.

At the long tables later, the air from the kitchen made the tent warm and humid, and Jordan sat between his friend Chance and a cousin of the bride named Mr. Byrne, who had married into the family years ago and clearly knew everyone. Rice dishes came around family style. Chance, who was busy telling a story about the school talent show, picked up the big serving spoon with his left hand and started to pass the platter. Jordan noticed something before Chance did: every other person at the table, all the way down both sides, was eating and passing with their right hand only, even the left-handed kid who had switched his fork over. It wasn't accident. It was a rule, the kind nobody announced but everybody followed.

Jordan couldn't see the rule itself, only the pattern, so he tested it the way he'd simulate a guess in science class, one trial at a time. He took the platter with his right hand and passed it on with his right. He accepted the tea with his right. Nobody corrected him. Nobody even glanced. Then Chance reached across with his left hand for the bread basket, and Mr. Byrne caught his sleeve gently and said, "Right hand, mate, right hand for eating and for giving things. It's respect."

Chance switched, and Jordan passed him the butter, right hand to right hand, like he'd known all along.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: A short circuit, a wire joining a battery's two ends with nothing in between, lets a large current flow that can make the wire and battery dangerously hot.
story:
Jordan had one D battery, one small bulb, a strip of aluminum foil, and five minutes before Mr. Hassan's mandatory science club ended for the day. He and Campbell were hunched over the picnic table at the edge of the playground, where pale lichen crept up the wooden legs and flaked off on their sneakers.

"Watch," Jordan said. He folded the foil into a tight wire shape, pressed one end to the top of the battery, and touched the other end straight to the bottom. The bulb sat untouched on the table, still dark. Nothing lit. Worse, the foil was getting warm in his fingers, then genuinely hot, and the battery itself was heating up like a stone left in the sun.

"Drop it!" Mr. Hassan's hand came down quick, knocking the foil away onto the grass. Jordan's fingertips stung and his heart pounded, but the teacher's voice was steady, not angry. "That's a short circuit," Mr. Hassan said. "A wire joining a battery's two ends with nothing in between." He crouched to their level, elbows on the table. "It lets a large current flow, enough to make the wire and battery dangerously hot. That's why I grabbed it."

Jordan stared at the foil lying in the grass, thin and harmless-looking. So the problem wasn't the battery, and it wasn't the foil. The problem was the empty gap where the bulb should have been, because the electricity had taken the easy road and bypassed the one thing he actually wanted to light.

"Can we try once more?" he asked. Mr. Hassan checked his watch, then nodded. Campbell scooted closer to hold the battery steady while Jordan laid one foil wire to the bulb's side and another to its bottom tip, and then to the battery, leaving the bulb stubbornly in between. The filament glowed orange. Campbell whooped so loudly that Madeleine looked over from the swings across the playground.

"Jordan made fire," Campbell announced, holding the battery up like a trophy. "On purpose this time."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand, mud or shells are pressed together and cemented over time.
story:
The three boxes on Mr. Popescu's desk said IGNEOUS, SEDIMENTARY, and METAMORPHIC, and the six rocks laid out in front of Lucas refused to announce which was which. Frederic had already dropped four rocks into boxes and was leaning back with his arms crossed. "I just guess," he said. "If it's shiny, igneous. If it's boring, the middle one." Lucas stared at a gray lump with faint stripes across its face and felt his whole premise wobble. Guessing had gotten Frederic a perfect score on the vocabulary quiz, but guessing felt wrong for rocks, because rocks had histories you could not see, and there had to be a way to read them.

Then he remembered the field trip to the quarry last autumn, the one where the class had stood at the bottom of a desolate white pit while the wind plastered their jackets against them. Ludovik had pointed at the cliff and asked why the rock was striped, like a layer cake tipped on its side. Nobody had answered that day, but the guide had said one sentence before the bus came: "Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand, mud or shells are pressed together and cemented over time." Lucas had forgotten it until now, staring at the striped lump.

He picked it up and turned it toward the window light. The stripes ran in even bands, and when he tilted the rock he saw something small and pale caught in one band, curved like a fragment of shell. If the layers were sand and mud pressed and cemented, then a shell caught between them made sense, the way a pressed flower gets stuck between pages. He needed to check the idea against more than one rock, so he carried the lump to Ludovik's table, where Ludovik was scowling at his own gray lump.

"Look at the bands," Lucas said. "Mine has a shell piece in one. Does yours have anything like that, grains or bits?" Ludovik held his rock under the light, turned it twice, and stopped. "There are little dark specks in the lines. Like sand." They compared the two rocks side by side, and both had stripes, both had specks or shell fragments caught in the bands. Lucas dropped his into the SEDIMENTARY box, and after a pause, Ludovik did the same.

Frederic came over and frowned at their boxes. "But the shiny black one," he said. "I put it in igneous because it's pretty." Lucas turned the black rock over. No bands, no grains, just a smooth glassy face. He said nothing, only set it beside the striped lumps so Frederic could see the difference himself. Frederic bit his lip, picked up the black rock, and moved it back to the igneous box. Then he grabbed the last boring gray one and held it up to the window. "Bands," he announced. "Sedimentary. And I only guessed twice."

Mr. Popescu walked past their tables with his clipboard, paused, and made three small marks. Lucas exhaled and slid the striped lump to the center of the box, shell side up.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
Bennett stood in front of the festival's heritage booth with a clipboard under his arm and a problem in his pocket. His class project was a graph of the cultural origins of people in his town, based on the numbers Mr. Bianchi had printed from the Canadian census. The graph looked wrong. His bars added up to one hundred and forty percent, which was impossible, and the project was due Monday.

The gym smelled of fried plantains and cardamom. Down one wall, tables held flags, embroidered cloth, and trays of dumplings that Maxim was sampling with great determination. Bennett needed answers, so he set up his clipboard beside Mr. Bianchi's table and began asking people the question on his sheet: "What origins would you say you have?"

A woman with a woven scarf stopped and said, "I'm Scottish and Cree." A teenage boy said, "Jamaican, Irish, and Chinese." Krish arrived with a plate of samosas and leaned over Bennett's shoulder. "You're counting people twice," Krish said. "No, I'm counting answers, not people," Bennett said, but even as he said it, the thought landed. He drew a quick chart on the back of his sheet: every person at the festival as one circle, every origin as a sticker on that circle. One woman had three stickers. His total counted stickers, not circles. Since 1981, the census had let everyone report more than one origin, so the totals could add up to more than the whole population of Canada itself.

He had wanted to evade redoing the graph all afternoon, hoping the numbers would fix themselves. They would not. So he sat on the floor behind the booth and recollected his count as people, not origins, keeping each person once. His percentages came down to a neat one hundred, and the bar for "multiple origins" was the tallest one on the page.

At the evening's climax, when the lights dimmed and the drummers started, Mr. Bianchi came over to look. Bennett held up the graph, feeling assertive for the first time all day. "It was never a mistake in the numbers," he said. "It was me, counting answers instead of people." Mr. Bianchi tapped the tall bar with one finger. "Put a label on that one," he said, "so everyone at Monday's presentation knows it's the whole town in there."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, which lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure people feel in their ears as a plane descends.
story:
Ryder lay on his towel at Marlin Beach and watched the waves convert the morning's smooth sand into a rumpled mess of ridges and holes. Tomorrow his family would fly home, and that was the problem. On the flight out, during the landing, his ears had felt like someone was pushing two thumbs against them from the inside. His little sister, Dree, had screamed the whole way down, and a man across the aisle had put his headphones on like a laser beam of annoyance aimed straight at their row.

He thought about last summer, the trip to his grandmother's house. Same thing. Landing, pressure, pain. But on the flight out to the beach this time, something odd had happened. The seatbelt sign had come on, the plane had started down, and his ears had popped and felt fine. What was different? He turned it over like a shell in his hand. On the way out, he had been drinking a juice box when the descent began. On the way to Grandma's, nothing. On the flight to the beach when his ears had hurt, also nothing.

"Could drinking actually do something?" he asked Anaeve, who was building a wall of wet sand with Ariella against the incoming tide.

"Drinking what?" Ariella said, dumping a bucket.

"Anything. On planes." Ryder told them about the juice box and the two bad flights. He did not mention Dree screaming, because Anaeve would do an impression of it for the rest of the day. She had a talent for impressions.

Anaeve squinted at him. "My mom chews gum on every flight. Every single one. She says swallowing opens your Eustachian tubes. She says that exact word, Eustachian, like she's proud of it." Ariella laughed so hard she sat down in her own sand wall, and the tide came in and converted the whole fortress into a puddle.

Ryder spent the rest of the afternoon running a test. Every ten minutes he yawned, big and fake, and swallowed, and paid attention to what happened in his ears. Each time there was a tiny click, like a bubble popping somewhere behind his jaw. Whatever those tubes were, they seemed to answer when he swallowed. It was like finding a secret button in a wall. He could not see it, but he could feel it working.

The next day, the descent home began with an abrupt drop that made the whole cabin go quiet. Ryder's ears started to press, and beside him Dree began to cry, kicking her sneakers against the seat. He yawned, wide, and swallowed, and the pressure in his own ears let go with a soft pop. Then he dug into the seat pocket and found the juice box their mom had packed.

"Hey, Dree. Look. Big girl juice." He held the straw to her mouth. She hiccupped, glared at him, and drank. Three swallows later her crying stopped like someone had shut off a faucet, and she pointed at her own ear with one sticky finger.

"Popped," she said.

"Yeah," Ryder said. "Mine too."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger, and in that case a person is actually required to eat or drink.
story:
Chase had never fasted before, not even for part of a day, so when his mom dropped him at his cousin Daniel's house on the morning of Yom Kippur, he felt like an explorer walking into unfamiliar territory. His stomach had already started a gradual grumble, and it was not even noon.

"You don't eat or drink until tonight," Daniel explained, setting a pitcher of water on the counter where it sat like a taunt. "That's the fast."

Chase watched his cousin carefully. Adults had told Chase that fasting was about saying sorry and thinking hard, but how could not eating portray anything? It was like a neuron in your brain, invisible but sending some kind of message anyway. He wondered what the message actually was.

Then he noticed something odd. Daniel, who had diabetes, kept glancing at the kitchen clock. At one o'clock, their uncle handed Daniel a glass of juice. Chase blinked. "Aren't you fasting?"

"Fast day," Daniel said, "but the rabbi told me I have to drink when my sugar could drop. When health is in danger, Jewish law waives the fast. In that case, you're actually required to eat or drink." He said it like it was the most normal thing in the world.

Chase thought that sounded backwards. He tested it out loud anyway. "So skipping it would be the wrong thing? For you, not eating would break the rule?"

"Exactly," Daniel said. "If I passed out, that's not holy, that's just a mess."

Their uncle laughed and ruffled Daniel's hair. Chase grinned and looked at the water pitcher again. He understood the fast now, but he still had one question burning. "Can I try it for just this afternoon, then?"

"Ask your mom," said the uncle, and Chase was already dialing.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The core shadow is the darkest band of shadow on the sphere itself, lying just past the terminator on the side away from the light.
story:
Ms. Hoang set a white plaster ball on each table and clicked on a single lamp, and Penelope leaned in so fast she nearly knocked over her pencil. "Today we generate light and shadow with graphite," Ms. Hoang said, "so watch the ball, not your paper." Penelope watched. The lamp sat off to the left, and the sphere blazed with a bright spot, then faded along a curved edge into grey, then deeper grey, then a pool of darkness lying on the table.

She shaded fast, eager to finish first, but when she held up her drawing something was wrong. Her sphere looked like a flat grey disc, like a coin glued to the page. Francesca, one table over, was frowning at hers too, and Roland had given up entirely and was drawing a diagonal stripe across his corner of the paper out of pure frustration.

"That's the exact same grey all the way across," Francesca said, tapping the dark half of Penelope's drawing.

Penelope looked back at the plaster ball. The dark half wasn't the same at all. The very darkest band wasn't at the far edge; it sat just past the curved border between light and dark, on the side away from the lamp. After that darkest stripe, the sphere actually got a little lighter again, like some faint bounce from the table. She tried saying the border out loud. "Terminator," Roland said, pointing at his own ball with sudden interest. "Ms. Hoang wrote it on the board. That line there." And the darkest band, Penelope decided, needed its own word, so she wrote "core shadow" beside it in her sketchbook, right where it belonged.

She started over, pressing hard only in that one band just past the terminator, easing up everywhere else, and dropping a soft cast shadow onto the table. Francesca leaned across the aisle to see, then erased her whole dark side without a word.

"Whoa," Roland said, staring at Penelope's page. "It actually looks round."

"Now do mine," Francesca begged, sliding her drawing down the table.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: An introduction often opens with a hook, such as a question, a surprising fact or a short story, to catch the reader's interest before stating the thesis.
story:
Landon slid his essay across the library table and watched Farah's face fall as she read the first line. "Our school should start a recycling club," she read out loud. "That's it? That's your whole opening?" Behind them, the librarian shushed a group of sixth graders, and somewhere near the biography shelves, Roxanne was supposed to be drafting her own paper but kept drifting over to look at Landon's.

"The assignment says five paragraphs," Landon said. "Introduction, three reasons, conclusion. I did the introduction. It states my thesis." He pointed at his notes, where he had written thesis and underlined it twice. "Ms. Berg said the thesis goes at the start."

Farah pulled the paper closer. She wanted her essay on cafeteria food read at the school board meeting next month, and she was determined to figure out why some papers made people sit up and others made them yawn. "Your thesis is fine. But you buried it. Watch." She flipped her own essay around. Her first sentence was a question: "Did you know the meatloaf has been in the freezer since October?" Then came a surprising fact about the lunch budget, and only after that did she write her thesis.

Roxanne leaned over both their shoulders. "It's called a hook," she said. "My cousin taught me. An introduction opens with a hook, like a question, a surprising fact, or a short story, and then it catches the reader's interest before you state the thesis." She snatched Landon's pencil before he could argue and wrote hook at the top of his page in enormous letters.

Landon wasn't sure he believed it, so he decided to test it. He copied his thesis onto three scraps of paper and wrote a different opening above each one: the plain version, a question, and two sentences about the dormant recycling bins sitting unopened in the supply closet since September. Then he asked a boy shelving books nearby to pick the paper he would keep reading. The boy chose the one about the bins. Landon tried it on a girl at the computers, then on the librarian. Both times, the story version won.

"It's like the bins were under siege by nobody using them," Roxanne said, squinting at his sentence. "That's not what siege means. Never mind."

Farah was already rewriting her own opening. "Ms. Berg said we get five minutes at the board meeting," she said. "If my first line is strong enough, they'll listen to the whole five minutes."

Landon read his new opening once more, then raised his hand toward the far corner of the library. "Excuse me," he called to a boy by the window, "if I gave you one sentence, would you keep reading?"

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: Slope steepness can be found by dividing the rise in height by the horizontal distance; rising 100 meters over 500 meters is a 20 percent grade.
story:
Ellie spread the map across the library table so fast that it knocked over Orion's stack of books, and he had to scramble to retrieve three of them from under the chair. "Sorry," she said, not sounding very sorry. "I need to figure out Hilltop Road before Saturday, because my dad says if it's too steep, we walk the bikes up it, and walking is for quitters."

"Orion, look." She traced her finger along a winding line. "The map has these brown contour lines. Where they're squished together, the hill is steep. Where they're far apart, it's gentle." She had read that in the atlas's front pages an hour ago, and it had felt like being handed a secret code.

Gurshan slid into the seat across from them and peered at the squished lines. "Squished how much, though? Squished isn't a number."

"It could be a number," Ellie said. "Everything's a number if you're brave enough." She checked the map's legend. Each contour line meant twenty meters of height, and the scale said one centimeter on the map equaled one hundred meters of real ground. She grabbed her ruler from her backpack and measured where Hilltop Road crossed the hillside. Between the bottom and the top, the road climbed past five contour lines. Five lines meant one hundred meters of rise. She measured the distance along the road: five centimeters, which meant five hundred meters of real ground.

Gurshan drummed his fingers. "So what's that in percent?"

"One hundred divided by five hundred," Ellie said, scribbling on the map's margin. "That's a twenty percent grade." She said the last part with a flourish, like announcing a magician's reveal.

Ms. Holloway, the librarian, paused by their table on her way past with an armload of returns. "Twenty percent," she repeated, and gave a low whistle. "That's a proper leg burner. Some riders can push up that, some can't. Depends on the rider." She raised an eyebrow at Ellie and walked on toward the front desk.

"Depends on the rider," Ellie repeated slowly. She looked at the map again, at the parallel brown lines crowding Hilltop Road like passengers on a rush-hour train. Then she flipped the atlas to the back page, found a beginner cycling book she'd noticed earlier, and pulled it toward her. "New plan," she said, turning to a chapter called Hills. "Saturday, I'm going to be the kind of rider who can."

"Or we take Maple Street," Gurshan offered. "The lines there are practically on vacation."

Ellie narrowed her eyes at him over the top of the book. "Orion, hold him down."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures, so a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent.
story:
Thomas had assumed a polling station would be boring, but Ms. Lombardi's class was there on a Tuesday because the gym was unavailable, and the assignment sheet in his hand said he had to explain how a bill becomes a law. Not a federal bill. A provincial one. He was supposed to interview one voter and one poll worker, and he had brought his two-column chart to fill in.

"Do you want to do the voter and I'll do the poll worker?" asked Ludovick. Ludovick's actual goal was the little round sticker that said I VOTED, which the clerk was sticking on every adult who came out from behind the cardboard screens. Ludovick had asked twice already if there were any spare ones.

"You can have my sticker if I get one," Thomas said, which was a compromise, because he wanted the chart filled in more than anything on his body. Yusuf tagged along to watch.

The poll worker, a woman with a lanyard and a pen behind her ear, was handing out a sheet that compared elections to the work of the legislature. Thomas read it standing beside the table where people signed in. The federal side showed a bill going through two houses before the Governor General signed it. The provincial side showed one house, then the lieutenant governor giving royal assent. He counted the steps twice. Fewer steps. A whole house missing.

"Excuse me," he said to the woman. "Did they print this wrong? Where's the other house?"

"That's the difference," she said, and pointed at the word unicameral. "All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures."

"So a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent," Thomas said slowly, testing it out loud. He wrote it in the box on his chart, then crossed out his first draft, which had copied the federal column like a lazy photocopy.

"The election here is volatile this year, so we're busy," the woman added, because a man was now waiting behind Thomas to ask about where his polling division had moved. Yusuf pulled Thomas out of the line.

"Out of context that chart made no sense," Yusuf said, "but you just fixed your whole assignment by counting."

Ludovick was already at the far end of the table. The clerk had set aside a single sticker on the edge, and Ludovick held it up like a trophy.

"One left," he called across the gym. "Split it with me?"

Thomas grabbed his chart, folded it into his pocket, and held out his sleeve. "You take the sticky half."

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: A standard six-string guitar is tuned, from the lowest and thickest string to the highest, E, A, D, G, B, E.
story:
Ariana held the guitar like it might bite her. Ms. Lindqvist had gone to fetch her tuning fork, which meant Ariana, Jenson, and Kierra were alone in the music room with Jenson's guitar and a pile of new strings.

"I restrung the whole thing," Jenson said proudly. "Took it all apart first. Very thorough."

"Too thorough," Kierra said, pointing at the pegs. "You didn't write down which string goes where, did you."

Jenson's face went through several stages. "They're strings. They're all basically strings."

"They're different sizes, genius. Fat ones and skinny ones." Kierra plucked one and it buzzed like a grumpy wasp.

Ariana assessed the problem, turning it over in her head. The fattest string had to sit where the fattest one belonged, lowest and closest to her chin. But which note was it supposed to be? She remembered her cousin complaining about this at Thanksgiving, muttering the notes under his breath like a spell: E, A, D, G, B, E. From the low fat string up to the skinny one. Two E's, which struck her as negligent planning on the part of whoever invented guitars, but it was the rule.

"So," she said slowly, "fat to skinny, it's E, A, D, G, B, E." She strung the fat E, then A, then D, and had just finished B when Ms. Lindqvist came back and struck her tuning fork against the desk.

"This," Ms. Lindqvist said, "is your E."

Ariana matched the fat string to it, tightening the peg in tiny careful turns until the wobble between the two sounds shrank to nothing. Then came the clever part, the part she'd read about: play the A string's fifth fret, and it should sound like the E string open. She tested it, adjusted, tested again, and worked her way up the neck string by string while Jenson and Kierra leaned in.

The final E shimmered, matched and sweet.

"Consumer of one perfectly tuned guitar," Jenson announced, holding it up, "reporting for duty."

"Thank you, negligent repair person," Ariana said, and strummed a big glorious chord.

Kierra put her hands over her ears. "Okay, do that again but quieter."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
story:
Victoria stared at the two pots of basil on the kitchen windowsill, one under a bright lamp and one in ordinary daylight, and both of them stubbornly the same size. Her science fair project was due in nine days, and her poster still said, in her best marker letters, "My hypothesis: extra light makes basil grow faster." The plants had other plans. Three weeks of measurements showed a plateau, the little green stems climbing and then just stopping, like they had decided four centimeters was far enough.

"If they don't grow, I'll be humiliated in front of the whole gym," she said to Blaire, who had come over with her own project, an intricate maze made of cardboard that was supposed to test whether her hamster could learn its turns. Blaire's problem was the opposite of Victoria's: her hamster, Peanut, kept solving the maze perfectly, every single time.

"Maybe Peanut's just smart," Blaire said, watching the hamster zoom through the corridors for the eleventh time. "But I can't prove it. He finishes the maze either way, whether he remembers it or smells the cheese. I want to show he learns, not that he's hungry."

Victoria flipped through the book their neighbor Mr. Henry had lent her, a thick one about the philosophy of science. She had only borrowed it because it had a picture of a laboratory on the cover, but one page stopped her cold. She read it twice, then read it out loud. "The philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong."

"So your hypothesis has to be able to lose," Blaire said slowly.

Victoria looked at her poster again. "Extra light makes basil grow faster." If the lamp basil stayed the same height as the window basil, her idea would be wrong, and the plants would show it. That was actually good. It meant her project was a real test, not just a decoration. But then she looked at Blaire's maze. "Peanut finishing the maze can't lose. You need something that could come out differently if he's only using his nose."

Blaire sat up straight. "If he learns, he should still solve it when I move the cheese to the end he's never been rewarded at. If he's just sniffing, he'll go to the old corner." She grabbed a piece of cardboard and started drawing.

Victoria got a fresh sheet of paper and wrote at the top, "What result would prove me wrong?" Then she measured both basils again, carefully, and wrote the numbers down where everyone at the fair would see them. If the lamp plant lost, she would report it, and that would hurt, but it would still be science.

Blaire set Peanut into the redesigned maze, cheese hidden in the new corner, and they both leaned in close. "Go on," Blaire whispered. "Prove me wrong."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to 20,000 pounds for a practical way to find a ship's longitude at sea.
story:
The departures board kept flipping, and Florence's flight to her grandmother's city was still three hours away. She sat on the floor by the big wall map near Gate 14, tracing her finger along the faint lines until Ariella plopped down beside her with a bag of pretzels.

"Find Grandma yet?"

"Almost." Florence tapped the grid of curved lines. "Latitude is the sideways ones, longitude goes up and down. If I get the numbers right, I can point to any city on Earth." She formulated a plan: pick a city, read the numbers, then find it again with her eyes shut. Her first try landed her in the ocean. Her second try landed her in the ocean too, which the map seemed to find funny.

Mr. Hamdan, who taught geography and was on the same flight, wandered over with his coffee. "Did you know sailors could always find their latitude easily, just by looking at the sky?" he said. "Longitude was the hard one. In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to twenty thousand pounds for a practical way to find a ship's longitude at sea."

Ariella stopped chewing. "Twenty thousand pounds? For a number?"

"A whole fortune back then," said Mr. Hamdan, and he went to check on his boarding pass, leaving the fact sitting there like unclaimed luggage.

Florence stared at the map. Latitude, the easy one, ran neatly sideways. Longitude, the prize-winning one, went up and down, and she suddenly got why the two were not the same problem at all, or at least she felt the edge of it, the way you feel a puzzle piece fit before you can say why. She checked her grandmother's coordinates one more time, carefully, because guessing had already dumped her in the ocean twice and checking was less tedious than drowning.

"Ten degrees north, eighty-four degrees west," she read aloud, and put her finger on the little dot. Ariella leaned in and held the pretzel bag out like a prize.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
story:
Sawyer pushed through the festival crowd with a roll of poster paper under one arm, hunting for the booth with the blue tablecloth. Riley's sign-language club had exactly one hour before the storytelling stage opened, and the poster still said, in giant letters, WELCOME TO THE deaf CLUB.

"There you are," Riley said, signing and talking at the same time. "Did you bring the markers?"

"Better," Sawyer said. "A question. Should 'deaf' be capital or lowercase? The banner outside the library says 'Deaf' with a big D, but our poster has a little one, and the booth next door has both."

They stood in the middle of the fairground, surrounded by booths where people described themselves in every way imaginable. At one table, a woman in a woven shawl was explaining that her embroidery patterns came from her grandmother's village. At another, a family had pinned up photographs of the old mill, and a sign explained that the town had nearly emptied out during the recession in the 1980s, when the jobs disappeared, and that new families had brought it back to life. Two teenagers at a mic were teaching a dance from their neighborhood, laughing when the crowd got the steps wrong and starting over without complaint.

Sawyer pulled out his phone and typed carefully. On the club's own website he found a page Riley had never shown him, and Riley read it aloud. "In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself."

"So it's not a spelling mistake," Sawyer said slowly. "It's two different words. Capital D is about the community. Lowercase is about the condition." He looked at their poster, then at the banner near the library, then at the club's flyers, where Riley had used the big D everywhere. "We weren't consistent. That's why it looked wrong."

He tested his idea against every sign he could find. The storytelling stage had a card that said "ASL interpreter provided by the Deaf community," capital D. A health booth had a flyer about hearing tests that used the lowercase word. Each one fit the rule, which meant the rule was real, and it also meant their poster was telling people the wrong thing.

Riley grabbed the markers. "Fix it before Ms. Adebayo brings her class by."

Sawyer printed the big D in gold, three inches tall, and Riley held the paper steady while the ink dried. Then they propped the poster against the front of the booth, stepped back, and watched a man in a hearing aid stop, read it, and flash them a thumbs-up. Riley signed "thank you," and Sawyer copied the sign, his hands clumsy but getting there.

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model in which electrons travel only in certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus.
story:
Cole spread his supplies across the kitchen table: a lump of clay for the nucleus, toothpicks, and three wire rings he had bent from a coat hanger. The assignment said his model of lithium had to show protons and neutrons jammed together in the middle, and electrons in the right places around the outside. He pressed the clay onto a cardboard square and squinted at it. The nucleus looked like a blob of gray gum, which was fine, but the wire rings would not cooperate. Every time he wedged one into the clay, it tipped sideways.

"You're doing it in vain if you don't fix the balance first," said Daniella, who had come over with her own half-finished model in a shoebox. She held up a wooden skewer. "Mr. Halvorsen said ours have to stand up on the desk by tomorrow."

Cole ignored her and kept poking the wire into the clay. The ring flopped again. Then it hit him: the ring wasn't the problem, the angle was. He pulled the wire out, bent a tiny foot onto the bottom of each ring, and pressed all three feet into the clay so they stood one inside the other like the lanes of a tiny circular track. The electrons, three seed beads, could ride those tracks without falling.

"Wait," Daniella said slowly, turning her phone toward him. "Why rings at all? Why not just scatter the electrons anywhere? It says here that in 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model in which electrons travel only in certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus." She looked up. "So the rings are actually right. Bohr was the first to draw atoms that way."

"So my wire rings aren't just decoration," Cole said. "They're the whole point." He slid one bead onto the innermost ring and two onto the next, then stood the model on the counter to test whether it would hold until morning. His mother's laser thermometer, borrowed to check that the glue on the base had cooled enough to accommodate the weight of the rings, beeped once from the drawer.

Daniella leaned in close. "Tip it," she whispered. "Just a little."

Cole nudged the cardboard edge with one finger, and the beads shivered along their orbits but stayed on their tracks.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Egyptian farmers used a shaduf, a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy weight on the other, to lift river water up to their fields.
story:
Lucy stood in front of the glass case, notebook open, and read the question she was supposed to answer for Mr. Owusu's museum worksheet: "Why did ancient Egyptians build the pyramids, and how did the Nile shape their farming?" The trouble was that she had missed two days of school with a broken wrist, and everybody else in her group already knew the answers. Emily and Avery had wandered off toward the mummy exhibit, and Lucy had exactly forty minutes before the bus left.

She started with the pyramids. A sign near a model of Giza said the pyramids were tombs for kings, built tall so the king's spirit could climb toward the sky. That part she copied down, but it felt like copying, not knowing. She looked at the tiny model workers hauling stone blocks up ramps and thought about how many people it must have taken, how much food they must have needed, and how that food had to come from farms along a river that flooded and dried on a schedule nobody controlled.

That was when she found the second case, the one about the Nile. A long wooden pole stuck out over a little model field, with a bucket hanging from one end and a heavy clay weight on the other. A boy about her age was tugging at the pole's rope, but it was bolted down, so his mother had to intervene before he wrenched the whole display loose. A small card next to it read: "Egyptian farmers used a shaduf to lift river water up to their fields." Lucy tried the lever herself, gently, and felt how the weight on the far end made the bucket rise with almost no effort. Her wrist, still in its cast and strangely vulnerable whenever she forgot and used it, did not have to strain at all.

She thought of hauling watering cans in her grandmother's garden, each one heavy enough to make her arms shake. If she had a pole like this, she could dip the bucket in the rain barrel and lift it without lugging anything. That was the real trick, she realized: the Nile flooded every year and left wet, rich soil, but the water sat below the level of the fields, and a shaduf could lift it up. Farmers who could water their crops beyond the flood could grow more food, and more food meant thousands of workers could be fed while they stacked a king's tomb toward the sky.

"Found you," Avery said, skidding around the corner. "Did you figure out your question?"

"Better than that," Lucy said, and pulled the lever again, watching the bucket swing up over the little green field.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In MLA style, an in-text citation for a novel gives the author's last name and the page number in parentheses, with no comma between them.
story:
Mila spread her library books across the table like evidence at a trial. Ms. Johansson's note, clipped to her essay, said the quotation was fine but the page number had to go in parentheses so a reader could check it. Mila had written the quote with nothing after it, which meant the note might as well have said, nice try.

Tia dropped into the chair across from her and slid over a book about a boy who sails a flooded river to find his grandfather. "This one's theme is easy. It's about not giving up."

"That's a topic, not a theme," Mila said, though she wasn't entirely sure what the difference was. She flipped to the page where the boy's grandfather tells him, "A river takes everything, and still it moves." She copied the sentence down. Then she stopped, pencil hovering. Where exactly did the page number go, and did it need a comma?

Vihaan arrived with pretzel smell on his sleeves and leaned over her paper. "You're being very diligent about one sentence."

"I have to be. Ms. Johansson said the quotes need page numbers the reader can check." Mila tried it three ways on scrap paper: (Carter, 44), (Carter 44,), and finally (Carter 44). The last one looked the least like a mistake, so she wrote it after the quote and sat back. Author's last name, page number, nothing between them. If it was wrong, at least it was wrong neatly.

The three of them spent another hour hunting themes, arguing quietly until a librarian informed them that whispering still counted as talking and the cease-and-desist would be enforced. On the way out, past the poster about screen hygiene that advised wiping your phone daily, Mila reread her paragraph one last time.

At school the next morning, Ms. Johansson paused at Mila's desk and tapped the parentheses with one finger. "Perfect. MLA style."

"So no comma?" Mila asked.

"Author's last name and the page number," Ms. Johansson said. "No comma between them."

Mila slid the essay to the middle of the desk, title side up, and moved on to sharpening her pencil.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Cats cannot make enough of their own taurine, a nutrient found in meat, and a lack of it can cause heart disease and blindness.
story:
The kitten was supposed to go home with Alexis by five o'clock, when the shelter's foster program closed for the weekend, and it was already half past four. She stood at the counter of the veterinary clinic with the adoption folder in her hands while the receptionist photocopied her mother's signature on the form that said the family could afford a pet. Her mother had joked in the car that they were not taking out a second mortgage just to feed a cat, and Alexis had laughed, but she was starting to wonder what a cat actually cost.

The problem was the food. On the shelf behind the counter, the clinic sold dog food and cat food in bags that looked almost identical, and the dog food was three dollars cheaper for a bigger bag. Paisley had told her last week that her cousin fed his cat dog food all the time and the cat seemed fine. Alexis picked up both bags and turned them over, hunting for a difference. She could not see one. The ingredients listed chicken, rice, fat, vitamins, a long list of words she could not pronounce. If the difference was hidden, then something in the cat had to be hidden too, something dogs could make for themselves and cats could not. She had read a poster in the waiting room while her mother filled out forms, and one line of it had stuck in her head.

"Excuse me," she said to Mr. Tran, the vet tech who was restocking the shelf. "Does this word, taurine, matter? It's on the cat food but not the dog food." Mr. Tran nodded and said, "Cats can't make enough taurine on their own, so it has to be in their food." Then he pointed at the next line of the poster, which said a lack of it could cause heart disease and blindness in cats. Alexis read it twice. So a cat could eat dog food for months and look fine while something invisible went wrong inside, and by the time anyone noticed, the damage would already be done. Paisley's cousin's cat was nine years old, and Alexis suddenly wanted to text her.

She almost did, standing there with her thumb over the phone, until Mr. Tran cleared his throat and tapped the clock above the counter. Four forty-five. Alexis grabbed the smaller, more expensive bag of cat food, the one with the lush picture of a chicken on the front, and carried it to the register. She had walked in thinking she would save money with the dog food. Now she set the cat food down and counted out the allowance she had been saving since September.

At the door, the carrier meowed, and Mr. Tran called after her, "Check the label again when you buy your next bag, just to be sure." Alexis lifted the carrier so the kitten could see out the window toward the parking lot. "Every time," she said, and pushed the door open with her hip.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
story:
Logan dragged the folding table into the driveway before breakfast, because today was his first day volunteering with the neighborhood collection, and Mr. Banerjee had promised him an official job. His mom had signed him up after he begged for a whole week. The morning smelled like cut grass, and the metal table legs clanked as he snapped them open beside the cardboard boxes labeled CANNED SOUP and PASTA.

By ten o'clock, trucks had already rumbled past twice, and Logan noticed something strange. Both trucks wore the exact same blue logo, a bowl with a swoosh under it, but one was from a city two hours south and the other from a town he'd never even heard of. "How can they have the same sign if they're from different places?" he asked Lewis, who was stacking cans with the speed of a kid who had eaten three bowls of cereal and no patience.

"Maybe they're copying each other," Lewis guessed. "Like rivals." Logan shook his head. Rivals wouldn't share a logo. He had a different idea, and he wanted to test it. When the third truck pulled up, its engine rumbling and hot air rippling off the hood, he asked the driver to hand him one of the paper flyers from the dashboard. The flyer had the swoosh bowl on it and a map dotted with tiny marks. Maely leaned over his shoulder, her synthetic jacket squeaking as she crowded in.

"It's called Feeding America," she read off the top. Logan traced the map with his finger, counting dots until he lost track. "So it's not rivals," he said, his voice rising. "It's one giant team. All these food banks everywhere, more than two hundred of them, all across the country, all on the same side." Hunger was the real adversary, and they were fighting it coast to coast. He grabbed a marker and wrote a new sign for the table, then held it up so the whole street could see: EVERY CAN WE COLLECT JOINS A NETWORK OF MORE THAN 200 FOOD BANKS. Mr. Banerjee laughed and rang the cowbell.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
Abigail sat on her grandmother's porch with the old accordion strapped to her chest, sweating like the thing was alive. Her objective was simple: play "O Susanna" all the way through without a single squawk before Sunday, when her grandmother promised they would play together. Saturday was her last chance, so she practiced for two whole hours, missing the same note in measure six about four hundred times. The accordion wheezed like an asthmatic elephant. "We're both exhausted," she told it.

Sunday arrived and measure six still squawked. Grandma winced politely and offered cookies instead of a duet. On Monday Abigail stomped next door to Kaden's house, where he was failing to teach his cat to fetch. "I practiced forever," she said. "Two hours. One sitting. And I'm still terrible." Kaden threw a bottle cap across the yard. "I studied spelling that way once, the night before the test. Crammed the whole list in one giant chunk. Then I got 'rhythm' wrong for the fourth week in a row." The cat ignored the cap. The fourth week in a row. Abigail wondered why that was.

She tried an experiment. Instead of one giant Saturday chunk, she played for only fifteen minutes a day, Monday through Friday. Could smaller pieces really add up to more than one big pile of the same time? It felt too easy. On Tuesday she missed measure six. On Wednesday she missed it twice. On Thursday, her fingers found the button without her even hunting for it, like they had been secretly practicing while she slept. She laughed out loud on the porch and scared a cardinal off the railing.

By Friday, "O Susanna" rolled out smooth and elastic, bending and swinging the way her grandmother's version did. On Sunday, Grandma put down her knitting, and they played the duet twice, then three times, and Grandma's slipper kept time like a metronome. "You've been at it every day, haven't you," Grandma said, eyes crinkling. Abigail grinned and squeezed the bellows shut. "Same total practice, Grandma. Just chopped up small. Want to petition the church to let us do this in front of actual people?"

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Glossophobia is the name for fear of public speaking, and it is one of the most commonly reported fears.
story:
Natalie's note cards were so sparse they were basically blank, and her speech was due tomorrow. Mr. Mwangi had written the recipe on the board: a hook to grab attention, three points, a closing that circled back. She had the three points. What she didn't have was a heart brave enough to say them out loud.

At lunch she watched Eugene draft his speech on a napkin, cross it out, and draft it again on his sleeve. "Mine's about why cafeteria tacos beat cafeteria pizza," he said. "The whole grade will vote. I'm aiming for a landslide."

"My category is 'something scary,'" Natalie said. Her hands had been shaking since Tuesday, which was ridiculous, because she'd known these kids since kindergarten.

Arman slid her his juice box. "My hands shake every time before I talk in front of people. Every single time."

"That has a name, you know," Eugene said, mouth full. "Glossophobia. Fear of public speaking. And it's one of the most commonly reported fears. Mr. Mwangi told me when I asked why my knees wobble."

Natalie stared at him. One of the most commonly reported fears. Not just her, then. Probably half the room. She did the math on her fingers: if everyone was scared, nobody would be watching for her mistakes, because they'd all be busy being scared of their own. She could test that.

"Tomorrow," she said, "when I go up, I'm going to look for shaking hands in the audience. If I spot three, my theory is right."

Thursday came. She walked to the front, hook ready: "Raise your hand if your hand is shaking." Dead silence. Then Eugene raised his, wobbling like a flag in wind. Arman lifted his, and so did a girl in the second row, then half the class, giggling. Natalie gave her three points about fear, closed with the same raised hand, and the room actually clapped before she finished the sentence.

Walking back, she passed Arman. "Three," she whispered. "Plus five."

"I counted eight," he whispered back, and wiggled his fingers at her.

activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: In 1838, the German botanist Matthias Schleiden proposed that all plant tissues are made of cells.
story:
Rosalie knelt at the edge of the pond with her notebook, because the science test was Monday morning and it was already Saturday. "Draw one plant cell and one animal cell," the study sheet said, "and label the parts only plants have." She could not draw what she could not see, so she had dragged Byron and Grace out here to help her interpret the green fuzz of elodea leaves she'd pulled from the water.

"Cells are too small," Byron said, squinting at the leaf. "This is pointless."

"Ms. Chen said pond plants have the biggest cells we can nearly see. And she said something else, something about a timeline at the museum. I can't remember what." Rosalie flattened the leaf against her notebook page and traced its outline. Grace crouched beside her and poked at a snail creeping along a stone, its little foot gripping like a tendon grips a bone, firm and pale.

"My brother went to that museum last year," Grace said. "He's notorious for mixing up facts, but he kept repeating one thing. This botanist, Matthias Schleiden. German guy. In 1838 he proposed that all plant tissues are made of cells."

"1838," Rosalie repeated, writing it down. Then she stopped writing. "Wait. My sheet says animal cells were declared after that. So plants got figured out first. A whole year before animals."

Byron leaned over her shoulder. "Then the parts only plants have must have been the easy part to spot. The wall. The green stuff."

"The cell wall and chloroplasts," Rosalie said, and she started drawing, a thick box around the plant cell and a thinner skin around the animal cell, labeling the wall and the chloroplasts on the plant side only.

"I said it was pointless," Byron said.

"You did." She added spiky green chloroplasts, then a fat nucleus in both cells. "And you were wrong."

Grace held the snail up so it faced the notebook. "Even he has no chloroplasts."

"Poor snail," Byron said. "No cell wall, either."

Rosalie closed her notebook and stood, brushing pond mud from her knees. "Grace, ask your brother one more thing before Monday."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
story:
Charlie had one goal at Jannat's house: win the negotiation over the last chocolate chip cookie before Jannat's little cousin Ben could claim it. Ben was four, loud, and fast for someone so small. Charlie was laying out her case, two cookies for him last Tuesday versus zero for her, when Jannat pulled her into the kitchen.

"Watch this," Jannat whispered, holding up a marble. "Elliott showed me this yesterday. It's from a real psychology thing, from 1985. You hide the marble, the kid knows where it is, then the kid leaves and you move it."

"That's just hiding a marble," Charlie said.

"Just watch."

Ben picked blue. Jannat put the marble in the red bucket, asked Ben where it was, and Ben pointed correctly. Then she sent him to wash his hands, and while he was gone she moved the marble to the green basket.

"Now," she said when Ben came back, "where will you look for your marble?"

Ben, dripping slightly, pointed at the red bucket with total confidence. "There!" He lifted it, found nothing, and looked personally betrayed by the bucket. Charlie laughed so hard she had to inhale a whole breath before she could speak.

"Wait, he saw you move it. Didn't he?"

"He was in the other room. That's the point. Kids his age mostly say you'll look where you left it, because they think everybody knows what they know. Elliott says from about age four they usually get it right. Ben's not quite there yet."

Charlie frowned. Was that true of all four-year-olds, or just Ben? She needed more data. She borrowed the marble, found Jannat's other cousin, age five, in the hallway, and ran the whole thing again, hiding the marble in a shoe, moving it to a plant pot. The five-year-old looked in the shoe first, but then, unprompted, marched to the plant pot and found it.

"So it's not age exactly," Charlie said slowly, counting on her fingers. "It's more like a switch that flips around then."

That night she wrote a note and slid it under Elliott's door, since he was apparently the prestigious expert of the street.

Dear Elliott. Today we did your marble test on Ben (4) and Amira (5). Ben said red bucket. Amira said shoe but then fixed it. Questions: Do dogs fail this too? Do grown-ups ever fail it? Also, is there a version with cookies? Urgent. Charlie.
